entry.title: [PATCH RFC 0/4] IPE: add a dedicated policy keyring

div.pre:
Add a dedicated ".ipe" keyring for IPE policy-signature verification, modeled after the dm-verity keyring, allowing userspace to provision IPE-specific policy-signing certificates. Systems that do not provision the keyring retain their existing behavior.
This RFC is based on commit 48f936e302a9 ("ipe: update the project and test suite links") from ipe/next so review can begin before the prerequisite keyring work reaches that branch. The series will be rebased onto a refreshed ipe/next once that work is available there [1].
The keyring readiness check currently follows the dm-verity and BPF implementations. A parallel keys RFC introduces keyring_is_empty() for this purpose [2]. A later revision will use the helper if it is available in the submission base.
Testing: - Built an x86_64 kernel with GCC 15.2.0 and Clang/LLD 21.1.8. - Passed all 33 IPE parser KUnit assertions. - Passed all 4 sealed-default keyring selftests under QEMU TCG. - Passed all 16 provisioning-mode keyring selftests under QEMU TCG with ipe.keyring_unsealed=1.
[1] https://lore.kernel.org/r/user3@example.test [2] https://lore.kernel.org/r/user4@example.test
Signed-off-by: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test> --- Manuel Huber (4): ipe: add the .ipe policy keyring keys: add KEY_SPEC_IPE_KEYRING Documentation: ipe: document the IPE keyring selftests/ipe: test the IPE policy keyring

entry.title: [PATCH RFC 1/4] ipe: add the .ipe policy keyring

div.pre:
From: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test>
Add a dedicated .ipe keyring for IPE policy signature verification, modeled after the .dm-verity and .bpf keyring implementations.
With this, userspace can provision its own keys into the keyring, then restrict it and activate it for IPE policy signature verification.
This enables scenarios in which a trusted userspace component generates an IPE policy, and creates an ephemeral policy-signing key pair, provisions its public certificate, and restricts the IPE keyring during the early lifetime of a system. The trusted component can then sign the IPE policy, destroy the private key, and load and activate the policy. During that phase, the system is considered in a trusted state whereas the system transitions into a possibly untrusted state afterwards, running arbitrary user-provided applications. In such a scenario, the trusted userspace component could reside on a dm-verity protected rootfs disk, and applications would reside on additional dm-verity protected disks. The latter disks would be dynamically attached and their dm-verity root hashes and/or signatures not known a priori to launching the system.
A concrete usage scenario could be Kata Containers, which enables running Kubernetes pods in ephemeral, headless utility VMs, possibly without systemd. The rootfs disk is static and known beforehand, but containerd's image layers might be acquired and transported into the VM using the erofs snapshotter and dynamic block device attachment using dm-verity.

entry.title: [PATCH RFC 2/4] keys: add KEY_SPEC_IPE_KEYRING
[PATCH RFC 3/4] Documentation: ipe: document the IPE keyring

div.pre:
From: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test>
Document the .ipe policy-verification keyring and its additive use after the existing trust sources.
Signed-off-by: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test> --- Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/ipe.rst | 41 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++++- Documentation/security/ipe.rst | 16 +++++++++----- 2 files changed, 51 insertions(+), 6 deletions(-)
diff --git a/Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/ipe.rst b/Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/ipe.rst index 9e82a2082b94..48ccad203301 100644 --- a/Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/ipe.rst +++ b/Documentation/admin-guide/LSM/ipe.rst @@ -238,7 +238,11 @@ unconstrained root, and deploying an "allow all" policy). These policies must be signed by a certificate that chains to the ``SYSTEM_TRUSTED_KEYRING``, or to the secondary and/or platform keyrings if ``CONFIG_IPE_POLICY_SIG_SECONDARY_KEYRING`` and/or -``CONFIG_IPE_POLICY_SIG_PLATFORM_KEYRING`` are enabled, respectively. +``CONFIG_IPE_POLICY_SIG_PLATFORM_KEYRING`` are enabled, respectively. IPE also +provides a dedicated ``.ipe`` keyring for policy-signing certificates that are +provisioned by userspace, as described below. The ``.ipe`` keyring is an +additive final fallback and does not replace the configured system trust +sources. With openssl, the policy can be signed by::
openssl smime -sign \ @@ -251,6 +255,41 @@ With openssl, the policy can be signed by:: -outform der \ -out "$MY_POLICY.p7b"
+Provisioning the IPE policy keyring +^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^ + +The ``.ipe`` keyring allows a system to provision an IPE-specific policy +signing certificate without embedding it in the kernel or firmware trust +stores. It is not linked into any process keyring. Userspace addresses it +directly with the ``KEY_SPEC_IPE_KEYRING`` special key ID (``-12``), which does +not grant possession of the keyring. + +The keyring is restricted while empty by default and cannot then be +provisioned. To provision it, boot with ``ipe.keyring_unsealed=1``. Userspace +can add a DER-encoded X.509 certificate and then apply a reject-all +restriction:: + + keyctl padd asymmetric "" -12 < policy-signing-key.der + keyctl restrict_keyring -12 + +Both steps are required. IPE ignores the keyring until it is nonempty and +restricted, so a partially provisioned, mutable keyring is not a trust source. +The restriction cannot be removed. More than one certificate can be enrolled +by repeating the ``keyctl padd`` command before restricting the keyring. + +Restriction prevents adding keys, but it does not prevent userspace from +removing keys or otherwise disabling the keyring. To lock it against further +userspace modification, drop its write and setattr permissions:: + + keyctl setperm -12 0x08030000 + +This retains the permissions needed for verification and inspection. +Provisioning, restriction, and permission hardening must be completed before +relying on ``.ipe`` as a trust source. + +Once nonempty and restricted, ``.ipe`` is searched after the configured system +trust sources. An absent, empty, or unrestricted ``.ipe`` keyring is ignored. + Deploying the policies is done through securityfs, through the ``new_policy`` node. To deploy a policy, simply cat the file into the securityfs node:: diff --git a/Documentation/security/ipe.rst b/Documentation/security/ipe.rst index 4490aed5918a..80f9893dddb5 100644 --- a/Documentation/security/ipe.rst +++ b/Documentation/security/ipe.rst @@ -248,11 +248,17 @@ policy updates have to be done rebootlessly.
To allow an update from an external source, it could be potentially malicious, so this policy needs to have a way to be identified as trusted. This is -done via a signature chained to a trust source in the kernel. Arbitrarily, -this is the ``SYSTEM_TRUSTED_KEYRING``, a keyring that is initially -populated at kernel compile-time, as this matches the expectation that the -author of the compiled-in policy described above is the same entity that can -deploy policy updates. +done via a signature chained to a trust source in the kernel. IPE can use the +builtin trusted keyring and, when configured, the secondary and platform +keyrings. This matches systems where the entity that establishes the kernel or +firmware trust store is also authorized to deploy policy updates. + +IPE also has a dedicated ``.ipe`` keyring for deployments that establish an +IPE-specific trust anchor from userspace. The keyring can be provisioned and +irreversibly restricted. IPE uses it only when it is nonempty and restricted, +and only as a fallback after the configured system keyrings. This keeps the +existing trust model intact while allowing a policy-signing key to be rotated +across boots without changing the kernel image or a broader system trust store.
Anti-Rollback / Anti-Replay ~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

entry.title: [PATCH RFC 4/4] selftests/ipe: test the IPE policy keyring

div.pre:
From: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test>
Add an IPE kselftest that validates policy keyring operations for both ipe.keyring_unsealed values 0 and 1.
For the default ipe.keyring_unsealed=0, verify that a) the special key ID resolves, b) certificate enrollment is rejected, and c) the keyring is not used for policy verification. For ipe.keyring_unsealed=1, verify that we can a) provision multiple certificates, b) restrict the keyring, then reject unenrolled and corrupted signatures, c) authenticate policy loads and updates with different enrolled certificates.
Since IPE is built in, keyring restriction is irreversible, which is why we can only exercise the initially sealed and unsealed scenarios via separate boots. To get full coverage, CI thus needs to spin up separate environments with respective parameter values.

On Wed, Oct 21, 2026 at 12:51:35PM -0400, Paul Moore wrote: > Just a quick point of clarification, you're using the pattern you > described for other keyrings, not necessarily a dedicated IPE keyring > described in this patchset, correct?
Correct. The .dm-verity keyring and the .bpf keyring both work like this: sealed empty by default, opened for a single boot via a kernel parameter, and only ever consulted once the keyring is non-empty and restricted. Manuel modeled the .ipe keyring on them after talking to Fan.
> I know you/Lennart/systemd made the decision to implement your own > version of IPE instead of working with Fan to augment the existing > implementation to meet your needs, so I'm not sure if you've also done > something with an out-of-tree patch, BPF, etc. to implement your own > keyring.
There is no out-of-tree anything and there is no keyring of our own.
RestrictFileSystemAccess= is a BPF LSM program that PID 1 loads. It denies exec, executable mappings and W^X transitions for anything that isn't on a signed dm-verity device or the initramfs. That's it. It uses the hooks BPF LSM exposes.
> As far as I'm concerned the decision of how IPE uses an IPE keyring is > up to Fan.
This is really not an argument. Manuel posted an RFC that follows two existing in-tree keyrings to the letter. Fan asked to deviate from them. I explained what that costs.
> Of course, fitting in with existing norms is important, > but if it causes IPE or existing IPE uses a lot of pain, that can a > good reason to diverge from those solutions.
Which pain? The keyring is dead unless the kernel command line opens it, and it is only consulted after the system keyrings have already rejected the signature. Existing IPE users see no change whatsoever.
Fan's reasons were that it "looks kind of awkward" and that fs-verity does it differently. I haven't yet heard a single technical reason to deviate. The properties we get and the other model loses are:
(1) Fail closed by default. Without the boot parameter the keyring is sealed empty for the whole boot and can never be provisioned. With the fs-verity model the keyring is open on every kernel that has it and stays open until someone remembers to restrict it. If nobody does, root in the "untrusted" phase enrolls its own cert and loads its own policy.
(2) The opt-in is per boot and lives on the kernel command line, i.e. in the measured/signed boot chain. A Kconfig knob can't express "this boot", only "this kernel", and a distro kernel with the option on is simply open everywhere.
(3) Activation is tied to restriction. The keyring is only consulted once it can't be extended anymore, so there is never a window where a half-provisioned keyring is a trust anchor. With the fs-verity model it is a trust anchor from the first key on and extensible until sealed.
(4) That's what gives Manuel's Kata case the throwaway key: generate an ephemeral key pair, enroll the cert, restrict, sign the policy, load it, destroy the private key. After that nothing can be added to the keyring and nothing new can be signed. With the fs-verity model the same sequence leaves the keyring extensible unless the agent also seals, and the kernel doesn't care whether it did.
Note that IPE's own CI already does padd followed by restrict_keyring on .fs-verity in the initrd (anchor-fsverity.service). So IPE relies on exactly this sequence today. The pattern just has the kernel enforce it instead of hoping that userspace gets it right.
So what does IPE gain from a keyring that is open by default and consulted before it's sealed?
> These days everyone is > going to implement whatever they please, but if you have > needs/requirements about how you want things to behave in LSM land, I > think it would be helpful to engage with us before you make a decision > and then start pleading with the LSM folks to adopt your approach.

- You read Daniel's bpf keyring series yourself in August, Cc'd the keyring folks "for obvious reasons", and had nothing to say about the model. The cover letter spelled out in detail that systemd would provision that keyring the same way as .dm-verity.
- On 2026-10-11 Manuel announced in the KEY_SPEC thread that he'd propose a .ipe keyring "modeled after the .dm-verity keyring" after "initial discussions with Fan Wu". You and linux-security-module were on Cc.
As for "everyone is going to implement whatever they please"... In May you told the bpf folks that "we just need to be willing to accept that we have different needs and show a willingness to accept different solutions as a result" [1]. I don't see why that shouldn't apply to systemd using BPF LSM.
Frankly, I couldn't care less whether IPE chooses to model the keyring the same way. It just means it can't give equivalent security guarantees. I'm confused why you have to speak for Fu and why you're so defensive about this.

On Mon, Oct 19, 2026 at 04:15:57PM -0700, Fan Wu wrote: > You might need to explain why the existing keyrings, i.e. > builtin/secondary/platform cannot be used in your scenario. Like the > firmware is not trusted?
As touched upon in [1], the scenario uses an ephemeral VM whose IEP policy would be assembled after boot. There is a mix of explicitly trusted dm-verity root hashes and possibly signed dm-verity layers which can vary per VM, so the final IPE policy would not necessarily be known ahead of time.
This specific scenario is Kata Containers on Kubernetes. Each Kubernetes pod runs in a headless Kata VM with a static dm-verity protected rootfs, while its container image layers are delivered dynamically as dm-verity protected block devices. The kata-agent acts as trusted bootstrap userspace and would author the IPE policy for that particular guest before starting its workload containers.
The firmware is trusted in this scenario. A public policy-signing certificate could be compiled into the builtin keyring or provisioned through the platform or secondary keyrings. Because the policy would be authored inside the guest, however, the corresponding private key would also have to be shipped as a static artifact in the guest rootfs and shared by every guest using that build.
Instead, the kata-agent would generate an ephemeral, per-guest policy-signing key pair, provision its public certificate, sign the policy, destroy the private key, and restrict the keyring before allowing untrusted code to execute.
A dedicated .ipe keyring thus provides a purpose-specific runtime provisioning path for this scenario. Once the certificate has been added, the keyring can be restricted against further enrollment.
I envision other scenarios with similar characteristics may benefit from a dedicated .ipe keyring as well.
I could elaborate more on this, e.g., on the how users' deployed container images translate to dm-verity protected image layers etc. (the erofs snapshotter is used and there is no filesystem sharing between host and guest, image layer transport is realized via block device attachment), but I am trying to keep this response brief. Some more breadcrumbs on the combination of containerd, IPE, Kata can be found in [2] and [3].

div.pre:
On Thu, Oct 22, 2026 at 01:25:36PM -0700, Fan Wu wrote: > Also, one thing I missed earlier: before the policy verification call, > please also check: > > ipe_keyring->restrict_link->check == restrict_link_reject > > so we make sure the restriction function is the right one.
I would advise against this. I'll explain why. Which restriction goes onto the keyring is intentionally userspace's policy. The two supported ones are:
keyctl restrict_keyring $id
seals the keyring for good. Nothing can ever be added again. And
keyctl restrict_keyring $id asymmetric key_or_keyring:0:chain
only allows certificates that are signed by a key that is already in the keyring.
This allows userspace to enroll a vendor CA during boot and let per-image certificates that chain to it be added later after the trusted phase.
systemd-keyring-setup uses that second form for .dm-verity, .fs-verity and .bpf and then drops KEY_USR_SETATTR, so neither the restriction nor the permission mask can be changed anymore while root keeps write permission to enroll chained certificates.
Both are proper seals. A restriction can only be set once as afterwards keyring_restrict() returns -EEXIST. So there is no way to remove it.
So whoever restricts the keyring is the provisioner and whatever they pick is the policy. A random root process after the seal can't extend the set of trust anchors either way. With the chain restriction it needs a signature from a key that is already trusted.
That's why .dm-verity and .bpf only test that restrict_link is set. "Restricted" is the state the kernel knows about. The policy belongs to userspace.
So it would be really nice if we could've the same behavior for all these keyrings. I think that this is a really nice model and allows userspace to have a kernel enforced policy.
Christian

I think there is one issue with the design pattern where keyrings are set up in userspace, that I have mentioned a few times already and I got documented in https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/latest/systemd-system.conf.html#RestrictFileSystemAccess= as well: they are trivially bypassable if the kernel has kexec enabled and it is signed. The security model relies on the "good" userspace running first, but if kexec is enabled, there's no guarantee that will be the case, and as far as I can tell it gives root trivial capability of overriding it and extending the trust chain as the attacker wishes.
IPE specifically was designed to avoid exactly that, and ensure userspace could not execute untrusted code, even with root privileges. With this enabled by default, userspace can just load the same signed kernel image, passing in compromised initrd and command line, and gain arbitrary code execution on the host, since only the kernel binary itself is verified, and anything goes for the rest of the kexec parameters.
This is of course not to say this new IPE keyring shouldn't be added. But perhaps it would be nicer if the default build flag was mutually exclusive with kexec being enabled? Not sure if that can be expressed in Kconfig though? default: yes-if-kexec-off, no-if-kexec-on
At the very least IMHO this relationship should be documented explicitly in the kconfig blurb, as it seems to me it's a major footgun to leave laying around, and users might not necessarily be aware of it.

From: Manuel Huber <user5@example.test>
Add a dedicated .ipe keyring for IPE policy signature verification. With this, userspace can provision its own keys into the keyring, then restrict it and activate it for IPE policy signature verification.
Gate creation of the keyring behind a new by-default disabled CONFIG_SECURITY_IPE_KEYRING Kconfig option. When created, the keyring is empty and writable. The keyring is used as a fallback after the existing policy trust sources only when it is created, non-empty, and restricted with restrict_link_reject.
This enables scenarios in which a trusted userspace component generates an IPE policy, and creates an ephemeral policy-signing key pair, provisions its public certificate, and restricts the IPE keyring during the early lifetime of a system. The trusted component can then sign the IPE policy, destroy the private key, and load and activate the policy. During that phase, the system is considered in a trusted state whereas the system transitions into a possibly untrusted state afterwards, running arbitrary user-provided applications. In such a scenario, the trusted userspace component could reside on a dm-verity protected rootfs disk, and applications would reside on additional dm-verity protected disks. The latter disks would be dynamically attached and their dm-verity root hashes and/or signatures not known a priori to launching the system.
A concrete usage scenario could be Kata Containers, which enables running Kubernetes pods in ephemeral, headless utility VMs, possibly without systemd. The rootfs disk is static and known beforehand, but containerd's image layers might be acquired and transported into the VM using the erofs snapshotter and dynamic block device attachment using dm-verity. While in that usage scenario, signing a per-guest policy with a pre-provisioned policy-signing certificate in the builtin, secondary, or platform keyrings would be technically possible, it would require including its corresponding private key in the guest build artifacts. Making it possible to use an ephemeral, userspace-provided key avoids shipping a static policy-signing private key with the guest rootfs.

The host attaches the snapshot block devices and passes the signed policy into the guest, where the guest simply loads and activates it against .platform.

entry.title: [PATCH v3 3/6] KEYS: Verify the key identity in __key_unlink_begin

div.pre:
When two keys have identical type and description, linking the second key replaces the first in a keyring. However, attempting to unlink the first key (no longer in the keyring) unlinks the second key.
This happens because __key_unlink_begin() calls assoc_array_delete() with &key->index_key, matching only on type and description rather than the key's identity.
Example:
keyctl new_session >/dev/null keyctl newring ring_a @s keyctl newring ring_b @s A=$(keyctl add user A ss %:ring_a) B=$(keyctl add user A qq %:ring_b) keyctl newring R @s keyctl link $A %:R keyctl link $B %:R keyctl unlink $A %:R keyctl show
Verify the key identity before unlinking, and return -ENOENT on mismatch, instead of unlinking the key with the wrong identity.

entry.title: [PATCH v4 0/2] ima: reject modsig when detached data cannot be supplied

div.pre:
ima_collect_modsig() supplies the file contents to the parsed PKCS#7 message as detached data. If the message already contains embedded data, pkcs7_supply_detached_data() returns -EINVAL, but IMA ignores the error. ima_modsig_verify() then verifies the embedded data instead of the file being appraised. This could bypass the crypto check if one supplies data with an already known valid signature.
Patch 1 fixes the verification path by discarding a modsig if detached data cannot be supplied.
Patch 2 keeps the exact pkcs7_supply_detached_data() error for a separate failed-modsig audit record. This part has been split out on request from Mimi Zohar so that the verification fix can be backported without this audit change.
